title: Hybrid token-fence with epochal pacing and per-tenant linearized backpressure
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Problem:
We need an admission/control primitive for Dedicated fleets that enforces per-tenant throughput contracts while avoiding cliff-edge demotions under bursty demand. Existing token-bucket and queue-first approaches either allow short bursts that starve the shared slowpath or immediately demote low-priority tenants, causing sharp customer-visible regressions.

Goal:
Introduce a hybrid token-fence admission controller with short epochal pacing and a linearized backpressure model:
- Enforce steady-state throughput guarantees per tenant (requests/sec and compute-seconds/sec).
- Allow bounded burst absorption within an epoch without breaking SLOs for guaranteed tenants.
- When overload occurs, degrade tenants smoothly using a linear degradation curve instead of hard drops or full preemption.
- Surface autoscaler hints (headroom pressure, burst demand) so autoscaler can proactively add capacity or shift routing.

Design (high level):
1) Token-Fence Primitive: each tenant gets a reclaimable token fence: tokens represent small fixed-size work quanta (e.g., 100ms GPU slices). Tokens are consumed at admission and replenished at contract rate. Unused tokens do not accumulate beyond a bounded window.

2) Epochal Pacing Layer: time is divided into short epochs (default 500ms–2s). Within an epoch we allow burst absorption up to a configurable fraction of the tenant's epoch budget. Burst budget is replenished gradually across epochs to avoid long-term overcommit.

3) Linearized Backpressure: when the fleet detects sustained headroom pressure, we compute a degradation factor per tenant on a continuous scale [0.0,1.0] proportional to (contract_rate - recent_consumption) and a fleet-level pressure signal. This factor reduces admission tokens granted (soft throttle) rather than immediately rejecting. Progressive shedding happens first via latency-based queueing (slower admissions) and then by rejecting lowest-degradation requests.

4) Cooperative Autoscaler Hints: the controller exports: headroom_pct, epoch_burn_rate, predicted_exhaust_seconds. Autoscaler consumes hints to pre-warm capacity or shift routing between Dedicated pools.

5) Fairness and Priority: tenants with firm contracts (reserved throughput) have their fences prioritized. Best-effort tenants share leftover capacity and receive steeper linear degradation curves.

Trade-offs considered:
- Complexity vs predictability: epochal pacing and linear degradation increase controller logic but produce smoother UX for customers compared to hard demotions.
- Timeliness: short epochs reduce tail risk but increase control-plane message frequency. We limit cross-cell sync to summary signals and keep tight per-router state local.
- Accounting granularity: using small quanta improves accuracy but increases bookkeeping. We tune quantum size (100ms default) to balance overhead.

Acceptance criteria:
- Functional: Enforce per-tenant contract to within +/-10% steady-state for 30-min runs under mixed workloads.
- Stability: Under 3x sustained incoming load, P95 latency for guaranteed-tier tenants increases by no more than 25% compared to baseline and error rate remains <1%.
- Smoothness: Customer-visible throughput for tenants in overloaded scenarios follows linearized degradation (no >40% step drops).
- Observability: Expose metrics headroom_pct, epoch_burn_rate, predicted_exhaust_seconds, per-tenant_degradation_factor.
- Rollout: Canary to 5% of Dedicated fleets, progressive 25/50/100% with rollback signal if error-rate spikes >2x.

Implementation plan (milestones):
- Spike (2w): Implement local token fence and epoch pacing simulator; run replayed traffic tests.
- Core (3w): Build admission controller library, integrate with routing gateway, add metrics and autoscaler hints.
- Safety (1w): Add fail-open/fail-closed config, watchdog to prevent over-dropping.
- QA & Load (2w): E2E load tests, compare against current priority admission implementations.
- Canary & Rollout (2w): Gradual rollout and monitoring dashboard.

Open questions:
- Optimal epoch length: trade latency vs smoothing. Propose default 1s; run ablation in spike.
- Quantum size sensitivity: default 100ms tokens vs 200ms.
- Backoff math for multi-tenant fairness: should degradation factor include past SLA violations history?

Artifacts & links:
- Design doc (draft): https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/INF/Hybrid+Token+Fence+Design
- Spike repo: https://github.com/redwood-inference/dedicated-token-fence-spike/pull/4
- Load test results (initial): https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/dedicated/token-fence-spike-results

Acceptance tests / QA checklist:
- Unit tests for fence accounting and epoch transitions.
- Integration test simulating 200 tenants with 5% reserved and 95% best-effort.
- Chaos run with transient node loss and autoscaler reaction.
- Canary dashboard with customer-impact heatmap and rollback playbook.
comments: 2026-02-21: Spike kickoff. Implemented local simulator that replays production ingress trace for 24h. Observed that epoch=1s reduces short-term headroom variance by ~18%.

2026-02-28: Design review with Runtime and Autoscale teams. Decision: keep admission decision at routing gateway to minimize KV-cache thrash. Runtime will expose compute-slice cost estimate per model variant.
2026-03-03: PR opened for token-fence core logic: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving/pull/1128. Needs security review for per-tenant state storage and potential DoS surface.

2026-03-05: Load test v1 (synthetic): 3x peak load, 120s window. Results: guaranteed tenants P95 latency +22%, error rate 0.8%. Best-effort tenants saw expected linearized throughput drop. Collecting more runs with different epoch sizes.
2026-03-08: UX/PM feedback: add metric to show predicted_exhaust_seconds for tenant owners. Also ask for API to allow tenants to opt into temporary burst-mode (trade cost for throughput).

2026-03-10: Implemented autoscaler hint export. Integration test shows autoscaler can reduce predicted_exhaust_seconds by 60% when adding a node in <90s. Next: finalize canary playbook and safety toggles.
